transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-09-07
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Rivera (Redwood SE), Olivia Grant (Riverview Head of Platform), Samir Kapoor (Lead SRE), Lena Ortiz (Security & Compliance), Diego Marquez (ML Eng)

Summary:
Redwood demo focused on org/project key strategies, adaptive rate orchestration, per-project burst credits, and tenant guardrails via API and Console. Customer asked about VPC/private deployment constraints, auditability, and p95 latencies under bursty finance workloads. Agreed next steps for pilot pricing, security docs, and a benchmark session.

Topics:
- Org vs project key topology and recommended playbooks
- Rate policies: adaptive token-level throttling, per-key concurrency, burst credits
- Sticky routing and fallback to compatible model variants
- Observability: token-level cost, traces, and audit logs
- Private deployment notes: KMS, SSO, retention rules

Action items (note: repeated in metadata):
- Ethan: run traffic sim
- Maya: send pricing + security packet
- Riverview: confirm pilot scope

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: All right everyone thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, that's Ethan on the call our solutions engineer. Quick roll call?
[00:10] Olivia Grant: Olivia here, hi.
[00:12] Samir Kapoor: Samir, hi.
[00:13] Lena Ortiz: Lena -- security.
[00:15] Diego Marquez: Diego — ML.
[00:18] Ethan Rivera: Great. We're going to run through a short playbook for org and project keys and then show the Console and a quick API flow. We'll keep it focused on your bursty finance workload that Olivia mentioned.
[00:34] Olivia Grant: Yeah, our main concerns are predictable latency for critical scoring, isolation of data, and audit logs for compliance. Also cost — we want to avoid surprise token bills during spikes.
[00:45] Maya Chen: Totally, that's exactly what the playbook addresses. At a high level we recommend a combined topology: top-level org keys for coarse billing and org policies, and project keys for per-application quotas and burst credits.
[00:58] Samir Kapoor: Quick question — how do you prefer to handle sticky routing? We have some models pinned in-house and others on the cloud, and we need consistent routing in a multi-region setup.
[01:10] Ethan Rivera: Good one. We use a sticky routing layer that can pin by org/project key plus a hash of the request — we expose a routing policy in the Console. You can map primary region -> fallback region and also set model variant fallbacks (e.g., quantized Llama variant) when capacity is low. It's all policy driven.
[01:29] Lena Ortiz: Is that routing decision logged for audit? We need proof of fallbacks and who changed routing.
[01:35] Maya Chen: Yes, audit logs capture policy changes and runtime routing events. We log model variant chosen, region, and latency bucket — logs are available in the Console and streamable to your SIEM via S3 or syslog connectors.
[01:45] Olivia Grant: And retention? We can't retain raw prompts for more than 90 days for regulatory reasons.
[01:52] Ethan Rivera: You can configure retention per-project; default is 30 days but for pilot we can set 90-day max and optionally redact prompts at ingest. Also offers KMS-backed encryption for keys at rest.
[02:06] Diego Marquez: When you say per-project burst credits, are those token-based or request-based? We sometimes have long generation jobs that spike tokens rather than RPS.
[02:15] Ethan Rivera: Burst credits can be token-based, concurrency-based, or a hybrid. For your use case we can set token-bucket burst credits so long-running generations consume the bucket; we also expose per-key concurrency ceilings to stop runaway parallelism.
[02:30] Samir Kapoor: How do you enforce p95 SLOs if batching interacts with latency?
[02:36] Ethan Rivera: The runtime does continuous batching but we let you set latency SLOs per route. For critical scoring routes you can set a strict SLO and the router will prefer lower-batch, lower-latency paths or pre-warm dedicated capacity — that reduces batching but increases cost. We surface the tradeoff in the Console with a cost/latency slider under Optimize.
[02:56] Olivia Grant: Can you show the Console for quota policy setup?
[03:00] Maya Chen: Yep, Ethan will share screen.
[03:03] [screen share begins — Console UI noise, a clicking sound] 
[03:12] Ethan Rivera: So here's the policy canvas. At the org level we hold capacity contracts, token allowances and guardrails. You can create project keys under the org and apply inheritance or override. I'll create a sample policy: project key "risk-scoring" with 10k token/day baseline, 50k burst credits for 24-hour window, and concurrency cap 4.
[03:37] [clicks] 
[03:40] Ethan Rivera: Note the policy simulator on the right — you can inject a synthetic workload and see how quotas and burst credits will be consumed. I'll simulate a 5-minute spike of 200 concurrent requests.
[03:51] Olivia Grant: Does the simulator model real-world token distribution? Our requests vary 80–1,200 tokens.
[03:58] Ethan Rivera: You can upload a CSV with sample token sizes and the simulator will replay it. We also have a built-in sample for finance workloads with tail-heavy token sizes.
[04:09] Diego Marquez: That's useful. Does the console show expected unit cost during the simulation?
[04:13] Ethan Rivera: Yes cost projection is part of Optimize. It breaks down cost by token, batching efficiency, and model variant. It also suggests quantization or smaller model suggestion if cost exceeds a threshold.
[04:23] Samir Kapoor: If we set an org-wide cap, how do you handle fair share across projects? We can't have one service monopolize tokens.
[04:31] Ethan Rivera: We have a fair-share allocator — projects can be weighted. The system enforces min and max slices and has a preemption policy for emergencies. You can also set priority lanes, e.g., fraud-detection lane gets preferential tokens during business hours.
[04:46] Olivia Grant: What about concurrency spikes from retries? We saw retries in our stack cause cascading load.
[04:51] Maya Chen: We recommend idempotency and client-side backoff, but we also offer server-side leaky-bucket smoothing and request deduplication for short time windows to mitigate retry storms.
[05:02] Lena Ortiz: For the private deployment option, is the control plane in our VPC or yours? We need to decide depending on compliance.
[05:09] Ethan Rivera: For Private, the control plane can be customer-hosted in your VPC or a hybrid where control plane is customer-managed and the runtime is in your region. We provide a packaged on-prem agent. KMS/HSM integrations are supported and we can do SAML SSO + SCIM for provisioning.
[05:25] Olivia Grant: Good. Can you walk through an API call example that shows per-key quota headers and error codes for throttling?
[05:32] Ethan Rivera: Sure. Here's a typical response for a throttled request: 429 with body {"error":"rate_exceeded","quota_remain":120,"reset_in":45}. We also emit headers X-Quota-Remaining and X-Quota-Reset. The Console maps those to alerts.
[05:50] Diego Marquez: Are those headers present when requests route to fallback variants? I want to see if the app can adapt to fallback quality.
[05:57] Ethan Rivera: Yes, we include X-Model-Variant and X-Routing-Region in the response so your client can log or adapt.
[06:05] Olivia Grant: Hypothetical: we want to guarantee that fraud scoring latency < 200ms p95, but keep cost in check. How would you recommend layering policy?
[06:14] Ethan Rivera: Create a dedicated project key for fraud-scoring with strict SLO, set concurrency min and max, pin to dedicated capacity during business hours using schedule-based routing, and give it a higher fair-share weight. Then use Optimize to recommend quantization only for non-critical routes.
[06:33] Samir Kapoor: Do you support canary rollouts of policy changes? We need to test quotas without impacting production.
[06:39] Ethan Rivera: Yes the Console supports canary percentage-based rollouts and A/B on policies. You can route 5% of traffic to the new quota and monitor.
[06:47] Olivia Grant: Can you demonstrate the policy change audit trail?
[06:50] Ethan Rivera: [click] Here's the audit timeline. Shows who changed what and a snapshot — you can revert to any snapshot. Also every runtime event is stored as an append-only log with immutable IDs.
[07:03] Lena Ortiz: What's the retention on those logs again?
[07:05] Ethan Rivera: Configurable, default 365 days for audit metadata, and raw prompts retention is separate as discussed earlier.
[07:12] Maya Chen: Quick pause — any questions until now?
[07:15] Olivia Grant: No, keep going.
[07:18] Ethan Rivera: I'll now show the API flow for provisioning a project key and applying quota via our SDK.
[07:24] [typing] 
[07:28] Ethan Rivera: POST /v1/orgs/{org}/projects creates a key; response includes key_id and example headers to send. Then PATCH /v1/policies/{policy_id} to attach token bucket and burst credits.
[07:38] Diego Marquez: We have a CICD pipeline that rotates keys frequently. Any recommendations?
[07:42] Ethan Rivera: Use short-lived ephemeral keys for CI jobs, rotate with SCIM automation, and attach roles to keys with least privilege. We also support automatic rotation hooks to your KMS.
[07:53] Samir Kapoor: One more on telemetry: can we get aggregated per-route p50/p95 and break down by model variant? Our internal SLA tooling expects that granularity.
[08:01] Ethan Rivera: Yes each route produces metrics with variant-tagged dimensions. The Console exposes them and you can forward to Prometheus/Grafana. We also provide prebuilt dashboards for p50/p95/p99.
[08:13] Olivia Grant: Behavior under network partition? If a region loses access, what happens to in-flight KV caches?
[08:20] Ethan Rivera: KV caches are per-runtime node; we persist the cache when possible but on failover we warm caches from a snapshot or allow graceful fallback to cold start. You can set sticky session TTLs to reduce cold starts.
[08:33] Maya Chen: Let's simulate a failure in the policy simulator — I'll flip capacity down for a region.
[08:37] [typing/click] 
[08:41] Ethan Rivera: See, routing policy triggers fallback to other region and model variant. The simulator shows increased latency but no hard errors — unless you configure a hard cutoff.
[08:51] Samir Kapoor: I see the latency bump, do you surface which requests were re-routed?
[08:54] Ethan Rivera: Yes the timeline shows re-routed request IDs and the chosen fallback variant.
[08:59] Olivia Grant: A quick security nit — do you keep a copy of customer KMS keys?
[09:03] Ethan Rivera: No, customer KMS keys remain in your control when you select KMS integration; we store only key references. For managed KMS we have strict controls and SOC2 attestation.
[09:13] Lena Ortiz: Regarding compliance artifacts, can you provide proof of pen tests?
[09:17] Maya Chen: We'll include the latest pen test summary and SOC2 report in the security packet.
[09:22] Olivia Grant: Good. Back to quotas: is there a way to do retroactive reconciliation if we mis-sized quotas and want to credit a project?
[09:30] Ethan Rivera: Yes, billing supports adjustments and we can issue usage credits for the pilot period. The Console also has a quota backfill tool for delayed events.
[09:40] Diego Marquez: For our ML experiments we'd like ephemeral sandboxes with pre-seeded models and temporary keys. Any patterns?
[09:47] Ethan Rivera: We suggest org policies that allow self-service project creation with auto-expiring keys and default sandbox quotas. The Console can enforce sandbox TTL and auto-delete artifacts.
[09:58] Samir Kapoor: Do you have any known issues with long-tail token distributions? We saw high variance in one of our scoring pipelines.
[10:05] Ethan Rivera: Long tails are common. We recommend a hybrid strategy: cap per-request max tokens, apply token-bucket burst credits, and use separate lanes for tail-heavy offline jobs to avoid disrupting real-time scoring.
[10:18] Olivia Grant: Can Optimize recommend configuration changes automatically? Like suggest lowering batch size on a route after seeing p95 breaches?
[10:24] Ethan Rivera: Exactly. Optimize runs a workload analysis and proposes configuration changes (quantization, batching, route SLO adjustments). It can create a tentative policy change that you can review and can be pushed via canary.
[10:36] Maya Chen: I'll show the Optimize suggestion panel — Ethan will pull a synthetic analysis for the risk-scoring route.
[10:41] [clicks/typing] 
[10:44] Ethan Rivera: It suggests reducing batch window from 50ms to 20ms for that route, recommended dedicated capacity during 08:00–18:00 business hours, and a suggestion to use 8-bit quantized variant for non-critical auxiliary models. Estimated monthly savings 18% with p95 maintained.
[11:03] Olivia Grant: Nice. Any limitations on model variants we can fallback to? Do you support custom models we bring?
[11:10] Ethan Rivera: Yes we'll onboard custom models. We run a compatibility check during onboarding to ensure kernels and quantization paths are supported. For some very new architectures we may require a micro-benchmark.
[11:22] Samir Kapoor: How long does onboarding a custom model take?
[11:25] Ethan Rivera: Usually 2–5 days for standard formats; if we need kernel work it can be a week. We provide a checklist.
[11:33] Olivia Grant: For the pilot, we'd like to test both hosted and private runtime. Can we run a hybrid where critical scoring goes private and less-sensitive stuff uses hosted?
[11:43] Maya Chen: Absolutely, that's a common pattern. We'll show a sample routing policy that pins critical project keys to private runtime and routes overflow to hosted with lower-cost variants.
[11:53] Diego Marquez: If we overflow to hosted during a spike, how do you ensure data residency? Some of our data can't leave certain regions.
[11:59] Ethan Rivera: The routing policy can be region-aware; we only overflow to geographies you've approved. For highly regulated data we recommend no-fallback or to a customer-managed private runtime.
[12:10] Olivia Grant: Can you export a JSON representation of the policy for review? We want to run it through our config scanner.
[12:15] Ethan Rivera: Yes every policy has a JSON/YAML export and can be stored in Git for review.
[12:19] Samir Kapoor: One last technical: how is KV cache invalidation handled during model rollout? If we push a new tokenizer or model version, dead cache could cause a mismatch.
[12:28] Ethan Rivera: We version caches by model fingerprint. During rollout we can either warm the new cache or invalidate on switch. The Console gives you a preview of cache-hit ratio impacts.
[12:39] Maya Chen: We're about halfway through, do you want to pivot to a quick Q&A or keep exploring the Console?
[12:45] Olivia Grant: Q&A is good, please.
[12:48] Lena Ortiz: For auditability, do log entries include request body hash but not raw content? That would help with privacy.
[12:56] Ethan Rivera: We include a hash and metadata; raw content is optional and discouraged. You can also configure redaction rules so only masked fields are stored.
[13:06] Olivia Grant: Regarding SSO, we've got Okta — any gotchas with SCIM provisioning?
[13:11] Ethan Rivera: Standard SCIM flows work. We recommend testing in a staging tenant first. Group sync and role mapping are supported out of the box.
[13:19] Samir Kapoor: How are incident alerts surfaced? PagerDuty? Slack?
[13:23] Ethan Rivera: Hooks for PagerDuty, Slack, email, and webhooks. We also provide a postmortem export and timeline.
[13:31] Diego Marquez: Can the Console enforce per-route input validation to prevent prompt injection?
[13:36] Ethan Rivera: We have built-in prompt sanitizers and a policy layer for input validation where you can drop or sanitize inputs before they hit the model.
[13:44] Olivia Grant: That's critical for us.
[13:46] Maya Chen: Quick demo of setting up an alert tied to X-Quota-Remaining: I'll create one now.
[13:50] [click] 
[13:55] Ethan Rivera: Alert created. You can choose threshold and destination. For example, send Slack when remaining < 10% or when burst credits dip below 40%.
[14:05] Olivia Grant: For billing — do you support invoice consolidation across org and projects? We want one consolidated invoice but with per-project line items.
[14:12] Maya Chen: Yes consolidated invoices with line-item breakdown by project and tags is supported. We also provide CSV exports for your finance team.
[14:21] Samir Kapoor: Can you throttle specific models rather than keys? We might want to limit expensive models globally.
[14:28] Ethan Rivera: Model-level quotas exist — you can set global model caps and per-project overrides.
[14:33] Olivia Grant: Any concerns with tokenization differences between your runtime and ours? We've seen small differences affect cost.
[14:40] Ethan Rivera: We publish tokenizer versions and have a tokenization emulator. During onboarding we'll run a tokenizer diff against a sample corpus.
[14:51] Diego Marquez: Does the SDK support streaming with backpressure signals?
[14:55] Ethan Rivera: Yes streaming is supported and we provide client libraries that expose backpressure hooks. This helps avoid client-side busy loops.
[15:02] Maya Chen: We should talk timing for pilot — Olivia, you mentioned wanting to start next quarter?
[15:07] Olivia Grant: Ideally yes, but we'd like a 4-week pilot to validate latency and cost.
[15:12] Maya Chen: We usually do a 30-day pilot. We'll scope a test plan: sample traffic, key policies, and success criteria.
[15:20] Olivia Grant: Success criteria: p95 < 250ms for fraud-scoring, no data retention beyond 90 days, and unit cost within 20% of current baseline.
[15:31] Maya Chen: Great, we'll document that and include in the pilot SOW.
[15:36] Ethan Rivera: For the benchmark session we'll need your sample token distributions and expected RPS per route. Diego and Samir can share that.
[15:45] Samir Kapoor: I'll export p95 targets and current load stats and drop them in the shared folder.
[15:51] Olivia Grant: We'll also want the security packet and SOC2.
[15:54] Maya Chen: We'll send both after this call.
[15:57] Lena Ortiz: One more question — can you redact specific PII fields at ingest automatically?
[16:02] Ethan Rivera: Yes, we provide field-level redaction rules and regex-based masks in the ingestion pipeline.
[16:09] Olivia Grant: Alright, looks good. Anything else from Redwood?
[16:12] Maya Chen: One last note: we'll include an example policy JSON for your config scanner and a starter template for project keys.
[16:19] Olivia Grant: Perfect, thanks everyone.
[16:22] Maya Chen: Thanks folks. We'll follow up with the packet and proposed dates for the benchmark.
[16:27] [call ends]

Note: transcription includes some mis-hearings and occasional product name variants ("Redwood Optimizer" vs "Redwood Optimize"), speaker overlaps, and some shorthand.
